children: Saudi Arabia said Friday it has shut the crucial East-West pipeline that had allowed it to continue exporting crude oil after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, saying it was attacked multiple times by drones fired by militias in Iraq.

The East-West pipeline can carry as much as 7M bbl/day of crude a day, 750 miles from Saudi Arabia's oil-producing heartland on the Persian Gulf to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, where the kingdom has been able to ship millions of barrels of oil to customers around the world.

The pipeline attacks come as Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen strengthened their hold on the southern Red Sea's Bab al-Mandeb strait, another key chokepoint for Saudi oil exports, taking control of an island in the strait and a nearby mainland coastal town, capping a series of swift gains in the area that are believed to have been guided by Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Attacks on the pipeline earlier this year damaged a pumping station and reduced capacity by ~700K bbl/day, and Saudi Aramco (
) restored the pipeline to its full capacity within days, but the latest attacks reportedly targeted several pumping stations.

Saudi crude oil production has already fallen to the lowest levels in more than three ‌decades, the International ⁠Energy Agency said Friday in the latest oil market report, declining to 6M bbl/day in August from 8.3M bbl/day in July and 9.4M bbl/day on average last year.

The latest developments ​could represent a major escalation in the Middle East war if oil supplies are reduced through a second major corridor that further raises oil prices; Reuters reported Friday that Saudi Arabia has asked the Trump administration for military help.

The Houthi advances and any significant damage to the East-West pipeline could boost oil prices toward $120/bbl, although the extent of the gains will depend on the extent of the damage, according to Hamad Hussain of Capital Economics.
Crude oil futures pulled back Friday in an apparent bout of profit-taking after a string of gains but ended the week sharply higher in reaction to the escalating Middle East conflict.

"Although much of today's price pullback appears attributable to talk of Middle East countries discussing a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and some bearish demand aspects to today's monthly IEA report, the larger negative driver in our opinion is simply a deserved market correction following this week’s dramatic gains," Ritterbusch & Associates said in a note.
On Friday, front-month Nymex crude
for October delivery dipped 2.4% to $100.05/bbl, front-month Brent crude
for November delivery sank 2.8% to $104.61/bbl, and front-month Nymex October natural gas
slipped 0.1% to $2.831/MMBtu.
For the week, Nymex crude and Brent crude jumped 9.4% and 8.5%, respectively, while Nymex natural gas fell 4.8%.
Oil supply disruptions due to the Iran war, along with Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, pushed the U.S. national average diesel price this week
for the first time.
Front-month Nymex ULSD (

) for October delivery jumped 9.2% this week to $4.9593/gal, on Thursday posting its highest settlement value since April 2022, and front-month Nymex RBOB gasoline (XB1:COM) for October delivery gained 2.9% to $3.3072/gal.
Energy stocks, as represented by the State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF
, gained 1.7% this week.
